Learning Objective
Capillary network
structure
Describe the structure of a capillary
network and identify types of
capillaries according to degree of
permeability.

Capillaries (Revision)
Smooth muscle in arterioles, metarterioles,
precapillary sphincters regulates blood flow
into capillary network
Blood flows from arterioles through
metarterioles, then through capillary network
Venules drain the network
Tortora and Grabowski, Principles of Anatomy and Physiology.

Capillaries
Vasomotion
Periodic contraction and release of smooth
muscle in metarterioles and the precapillary
sphincters causes intermittent flow and
cessation of flow in individual capillaries.
Average blood flow across a
capillary bed
The intermittent flow in individual capillaries
averaged across a capillary bed in an area of
tissue results in a continuous (generally) non-
pulsatile flow of blood through the tissue.
Tortora and Grabowski, Principles of Anatomy and Physiology.

Capillaries
Vasomotion regulation
Decreased tissue oxygen drives:
more frequent periods of flow through
individual capillaries.
long periods of flow within each capillary
The net effect being increased blood flow to
the tissue bed.
Tortora and Grabowski, Principles of Anatomy and Physiology.

Capillaries (Revision)
Capillary wall consists of endothelial cells on a
basement membrane.
Capillary types classified by diameter and
permeability:
Continuous
Do not have fenestrae
Fenestrated
Have pores
Sinusoidal
Large diameter with large
fenestrae
Fenestrated and sinusoidal capillaries allow
absorption and filtration of water and ions from
blood to other body cells.

Endothelial cells of capillaries: caveloae and intercellular
clefts
Intercellular clefts
channel between adjacent endothelial cells
≈
width: 6 to 7 nm (slightly smaller than albumin)
allow transport of water and water soluble ions
Caveolae ("small caves")
a.k.a. plasmalemmal vesicles. Made of caveolins,
proteins associated with cholesterol and sphingolipids.
can carry larger proteins into the cell
can join to form vesicular channels through the cell

clefts
The nature of the
blood brain barrier:
tight junctions at intercellular
endothelium and capillary
clefts. Only small molecules can pass through capillary
pores var ies between

Interstitium constituents
List the constituents of the
interstitium.
See this week's on-line module in
iLearn.


The interstitium
The insterstitium is the space between cells.
It constitutes about 15 to 20% of the body
volume.
It is made up of...
Solid elements
collagen fibres
provide tensional strength in the tissue
proteoglycan filaments
extremely thin, providing a "brush
pile" (mat) in the interstitium.
Gel
Surrounding proteoglycan filaments.
Similar protein constituents as plasma.
Along with collagen, provides the bulk of the interstitium.
Free fluid
small channels of fluid throughout the interstitia.
Image: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology.


Lymphatic system
Describe the function and broad
anatomy of the lymphatic system.
See this week's on-line module in
iLearn.


Lymphatic system
Function: Reabsorb extravascular
Discovered at the same time that William
proteins, colloids, and
Harvey (re)discovered the circulation.
particulates and return them to
But much less researched as a whole than
the vascular space.
even vascular endothelial cells.
Total fluid flow through lymph is around 2 to
3 L/day (≈120 ml/hr).
Yet if all lymph flow stops, death will follow in
as little as 24 hours.


Lymphatic system
Structure of the lymphatic system
In all tissue.
Superficial skin, central nervous system,
muscle endomysium and bones carry only
pre-lympahatics, which in turn drain into the
lymphatic system (or, in the brain, to the
cerebrospinal fluid).
Lower body and left upper body drain by the
thoracic duct into the left internal jugular and
subclavian vein.
Upper right body drains by the lymph duct in
the right internal jugular and subclavian vein.
Image: Dorland's Medical Dictionary.


Lymphatic system
Structure of the lymphatic system. Lymphatic capillar ies.
Formed by single layer of endothelial cells.
Anchored by collagen filaments.
Overlapping of endothelial cells forms a
valve-like structure, reducing retrograde flow.
Image: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology.


Lymphatic system
Lymph flow. The lymphatic capillary pump.
As fluid enters the interstitial space, the
tissue swells and pulls on the lymphatic
capillary anchoring fibres.
This allows fluid to flow into the capillary.
As fluid exits the tissue, swelling decreases,
compressing the lymphatic capillary (may
also be assisted by external pressures on the
tissue).
Image: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology.


Lymphatic system
Lymph flow. Lymphatic pump.
Lymph vessels contain smooth muscle.
This mechanism is able to pump lymph from
The smooth muscle responds to stretch (as
one segment to the next. In larger lymph
the lymph vessel fills with fluid) by
vessels (e.g. the thoracic duct), pressures as
contracting. high as 50 to 100 mmHg can be generated.
This pumps fluid past the next valve, into the
next segment, stretching smooth muscle in
that segment.


Lymphatic system
Lymph flow. External compression of the lymphatics.
Lymphatic vessels may be compressed by
external elements, promoting flow of lymph:
skeletal muscle
arteries adjacent to lymphatics
things external to the body (tight clothing)

Lymphoedema
Tissue swelling due to inadequate lymph drainage.
May not solely be `lymphatic’.
Can be due to any in-balance in the Starling’s forces causing insterstitial volume to increase.
Image: Principles and Practice of Lymphedema Surgery. Cheng MH, Chang DW, Patel KM (Editors). Elsevier Inc, Oxford, United
Kingdom. July 2015.


Lymphoedema
Disease presentation
Swelling of limb
Limb feels heavy or tight or aches
Restricts motion of limb
Recurring infection
Hardening / thickening of the skin
Image: Principles and Practice of Lymphedema Surgery. Cheng MH, Chang DW, Patel KM (Editors). Elsevier Inc, Oxford, United
Kingdom. July 2015.
